newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: YEAREND-Lithuanian banks hope for positive 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Lithuanian banks hope for positive 1997.

text.p: One year after the Baltic state of Lithuania was jarred by the shock of a severe banking crisis and forced into sectoral restructuring, bankers are looking forward to a more positive 1997.
"We expect to see a lot of changes in the sector in 1997," said Raimondas Kutra, the deputy chairman of the country's leading bank, Vilnius Bank.
This year has been a period of stabilisation and consolidation for much of the sector after the crisis that hit the country at the end of 1995.

Bankers said 1997 would be a year when mergers may take place as banks try to meet central bank requirements, state banks are privatised and banks have to develop services as easy profits from government securities disappear.
The crisis was sparked by the closure of two of Lithuania's top banks, Innovation Bank and Litimpeks, which caused sector-wide problems and a government-backed restructuring.
"The worst is behind Lithuania now but more reforms are needed in the banking sector," said International Monetary Fund (IMF) Lithuania resident representative Domenico Fannizza.
"It was not just a problem of insolvency, it was a structural crisis," he added.
The previous government was forced to launch a restructuring of other banks and created a bad-debt organisation to manage the unrecoverable credits of troubled state banks.
The central bank responded to the crisis by tightening regulation, focussing on requirements such as monthly audited reports, increased share capital and better credit control.
"The rules were very lax when commercial banks began operations in 1991-1992," said Lithuanian central bank deputy governor Jonas Niaura.
He said there was too much "inside lending" as companies would set up banks to lend to shareholders without checking their ability to pay.

Now recovery is evident: Interest rates are down to nine to 12 percent after soaring to 40 percent, and bank assets rebounded to 6.4 billion litas at October-end versus 5.6 billion litas in June and 6.2 billion litas at the end of 1995.
Deposits also recovered, reaching 4.6 billion litas at the end of October after falling to 4.1 billion litas in February.
Innovation Bank remains closed but Litimpeks was reopened and is now trying to rebuild its credibility. Lithuania has 27 registered banks and 15 are in various stages of bankruptcy.
Of the other 12, three are state-owned and only six of the nine private banks meet all the central bank's requirements.
"From January 1, all banks will have to comply with all the regulations and standards, including international accounting methods and monthly audited reports," Niaura added.
The minimum share capital level will be raised to 20 million litas next year from 10 million litas.
"Some smaller banks may have difficulties meeting all of these requirements and so we expect some mergers," Niaura said.
The three large state banks, Savings Bank, the State Commercial Bank and the Agriculture Bank, accounted for 52 percent of all deposits at the end of October.
A shakeup is expected here as the previous government committed itself to privatising them although the new government has said it may hedge on Savings Bank.
Another positive sign is the quantity of foreign investment -- the central bank says 31 percent of the share capital in the banking system is owned by foreigners.
Leading bank Vilnius Bank is 87 percent foreign-owned and Poland's Kredyt Bank recently opened a branch.
"We have had enquiries from several other foreign banks," Niaura added.
But local distrust remains high as a survey showed that only three percent of people trusted banks.
